chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
title: Swimming in the river, jail and his mother's whipping
summary: He was a history-loving student who learned to swim in the Mississippi, was jailed at eleven with other boys, and was beaten by his mother.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: In a sense, I was a good average student. I was always a good talking type of person. I could always rap pretty good, as you would say. My subjects were history. I wasn't a very good mathematician, not even today, but I liked math, but I never would take the time to concentrate on it. But I can do it pretty good now, after growing up working in business with it. But I was mostly into history, and geography, and technical things like that. And then, see, I learned how to swim in the Mississippi River. I remember, as I grew up, when I was about eleven years of age, they caught me swimming in the river. We couldn't afford a swimsuit. I had an old, cut-off pair of pants, but I lost them. And when I got out the water, this white police officer saw me, and I would stand up in the nude, and they put me in jail. In fact, they put all of us black guys in jail on the west back of the river. Well, the guy who a lot of people remember over there mostly was a guy by the name of B.H. Miller, B.R. Miller Sr., who was the chief of police at that particular time. Of course, I got along pretty good with B.H. because the house on Fifth Street was right across the street from the jailhouse. And whenever my father thought I was doing something bad, they would tell me, I'm going to have the police to come get you. Whenever I saw that automobile, I saw him with that big hat on, before I would run. I was scared of the police for a while. Until I started growing up and realized that as long as I wasn't doing anything, the man wasn't going to bother me.
What happened when the cops got you, picked you up from the-

Well, they locked me up over in the jail across the house, and so one of the officers went and got my mother. And that's when I found out what Amazing Grace was all about. My mother beat my behind from a can of tomato paste to Amazing Grace. That's when I found out what Amazing Grace was all about. Boy, did I hoop and holler that day. And I started being good after that. I think I have marks on the back of my rear end right now because, see, my mother had a cat of nine tails. I don't know if you ever saw anything like that. It was a strap with nine pieces of thin leather cut. And then my mother had a wire put into the tips. And I had marks on the back of my behind where she used to- I thought my mother hated me for a while. But as I grew somewhere in time, my mother really loved me. I realized what she was really doing as I grew. She was trying to make me become, I guess, the man that I am today to go to school, to go to college, and to do constructive things. My Jewish association is coming out with me. I'm going to talk with my hands, Ted. That happens sometime. I have a lot of Jewish friends also. So that's- So did you talk with your hands? Yeah. I got a little too close to the microphone.
